video.title: How to Make $1M+ With a Drone ($1.5K in 30 Minutes)

summary: The Koerner Office hosts discuss drone roof inspections as a possible side business, covering customers, reported market trends, startup requirements, job delivery, pricing and customer acquisition. They describe additional services such as construction-site inventory checks and social media footage, plus separate examples including aerial photo sales and storm debris removal. Their central recommendation is to start part-time, build on existing industry relationships, and expand services after earning a customer's trust. Most operating figures come from the hosts' research or stories about other people rather than a directly interviewed operator.

speakers.name: Nick
speakers.description: Named by Chris in the conversation; surname not stated.

ideas.name: Drone roof and property inspections
ideas.one_liner: Capture and analyze aerial imagery for organizations that need roof or property condition documentation.
ideas.business_model: Per-job fees, with possible recurring contracts and add-on services.
ideas.customer: Insurance companies and adjusters, roofing businesses, property managers, commercial real estate owners, construction and solar companies, home inspectors, facilities managers, schools, universities, churches, and other organizations managing property.
ideas.problem: Manual roof inspections can be dangerous, time-consuming, and hard to staff; property owners and managers still need condition records and inspection data.
ideas.offer: Plan a drone flight, capture roof or site imagery, analyze the imagery with software and human review, and provide files or a report. The hosts suggest calling the service roof condition documentation in some jurisdictions instead of an inspection.

pricing.model: Per-job, per-square-foot, and potential recurring contracts.

price_points.label: Thermal imaging add-on; transcript renders the range as 1 to $3300
3D mapping or AI-powered damage analysis; transcript renders the range as $4 to $700

pricing.notes: These are figures stated by the hosts, not verified prices. The captions render the thermal imaging and 3D mapping ranges ambiguously, so they are recorded as spoken rather than corrected.

acquisition_channels.details: Start by listing people already known in construction, roofing, insurance, real estate, and facilities management. The hosts recommend piggybacking on existing relationships and referral partners.

Build location-specific pages with relevant keywords and city names, and optimize the Google Business Profile. They mention ranking for searches such as drone roof inspection near me and suggest drone facade inspection as a less expensive keyword.
Add photos and videos, solicit reviews, and ask for reviews after every job. The hosts say local leads can come from the profile before a visitor clicks through to the website.
Bid on local and service-specific Google Ads terms. The hosts say broad roof inspection terms can be expensive and suggest narrower location or facade terms.
The hosts discuss Facebook Ads for B2B customers and cite reported return-on-ad-spend examples. Their suggested validation approach is to test messaging with a limited budget.
Post short drone clips and before-and-after footage. They suggest reusing the footage across social platforms and websites.
Publish engaging drone footage on YouTube, which the hosts say can support discovery and search visibility.
Use companies that farm out drone jobs to local operators to gain flight experience and practice before selling directly.

ideas.delivery: The operator checks airspace and any required approvals, checks weather, reviews the roof layout on Google Maps, prepares equipment, flies the drone, exports and uploads the files, runs the images through analysis software, checks the results, and sends the deliverable to the customer. The hosts describe the operator being on site for about two hours and say an individual may manage around two roofs per day after administrative work. A human remains responsible for flight planning, safe operation, interpreting results, and client satisfaction.
unit_economics_claims: The hosts state gross margins of 50–70%, net margins of 20–30%, and a possible 40–50% net margin for a highly efficient operator.
They report DJI Mavic 3 prices of $1,200–$3,500 and startup costs below $10,000.
They describe a reported operator who takes 15 minutes to photograph a roof, captures 50–60 photos, and can inspect two roofs on one battery.
They report that the operator reached seven figures in annual revenue after four years and earns $15,000–$30,000 in inspections during a storm.
They say this operator has a few employees and two or three crews, and that customers replace about half of their manual roof inspections.
They estimate that an individual operator may manage about two roofs per day after preparation and administrative work.
They state Google lead costs of $30–$40 per lead and a 50% close rate, alongside a separate $70–$80 cost-per-acquisition figure.
They cite Facebook Ads return-on-ad-spend examples of 3:1 and 5:1.
ideas.startup_cost: The hosts estimate less than $10,000 to get started, including a DJI Mavic 3 costing $1,200–$3,500, insurance, and software. They also mention a $175 FAA Part 107 test fee. These are their claims, not independently verified figures.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated. They suggest starting part-time, using outsourced drone jobs to build experience, and drawing on existing relationships to pursue the first sale.

acquisition.how: SEO, Google Business Profile, paid search, paid social, and reusable video can generate and route inbound leads with software. Winning B2B contracts and maintaining referral relationships still need human judgment and sales.

onboarding.how: Forms and scheduling could collect site details and book jobs, but the operator must confirm site access, airspace, weather, roof type, and the client's needs.

delivery.how: A licensed operator must plan and supervise the physical drone flight and review the images. Software can assist with sorting and damage analysis, but the transcript says a human still needs to understand what to look for.

billing.how: Per-job invoices and recurring contracts could be handled by ordinary billing software with routine checks; no billing system is described in the transcript.

support.how: Automated status updates and file delivery could handle routine questions, but customers may need a human to explain findings, resolve image-quality issues, or arrange a follow-up.

uk_applicability.notes: UK property owners and managers have comparable needs for roof and site documentation. The FAA Part 107, US insurance statistics, and US licensing terminology in the discussion do not transfer directly; an operator would need to meet applicable UK aviation and property requirements.

risks: Drone flights require training, permissions where applicable, airspace checks, weather checks, insurance, and safe operating practices.

The speakers say some jurisdictions may impose additional licensing when a service is described as an inspection; that claim should be checked against local rules before naming or selling the service.
Metal roofs can interfere with signal, according to the hosts' account of an operator's learning curve.
The transcript describes confrontational onlookers and reports that complaints could threaten an operator's license; filming from a public place does not itself resolve privacy or consent concerns.
A drone operator still has to interpret roof condition and deliver acceptable imagery; automated analysis does not remove the need for competent human review.
The hosts say an individual may be limited to about two roofs per day once preparation, travel, file handling, and administration are included.
Work can depend on weather and storm activity. The hosts say storms can bring high volume, but that creates uneven demand and travel needs.
The hosts give an ambiguous captioned range for thermal imaging and 3D mapping, so those price claims are uncertain.
The hosts' suggestions about using customer footage for social content and capturing property images should be handled with customer permission and appropriate privacy practices.

ideas.name: Aerial property photographs sold as prints
ideas.one_liner: Photograph farms or homes from the air, print attractive images, and sell them directly to the property owner.
ideas.customer: Farmers and property owners who value attractive aerial images of their land or home.
ideas.problem: The owner may not have access to a distinctive aerial image of their property.
ideas.offer: Capture aerial images, develop or print them, and sell a finished image directly to the owner. The hosts recount Clark using model airplanes and a darkroom to sell large photos of farmland, then suggest adapting the idea with drone photos.

pricing.notes: The reported sale price is from Clark's historical model-plane photography business. The hosts' suggested modern drone adaptation has no stated price.

acquisition_channels.details: Clark went to the farmer's front door, showed the property photograph, and asked for the sale.

ideas.delivery: Clark reportedly flew a model airplane with a camera over farmland, retrieved and developed the photographs himself in a darkroom, and delivered large prints. The hosts suggest a modern operator could take a homeowner's photo while already working on the property, then arrange a printed copy.
unit_economics_claims: The story says Clark charged $250 for a print and had a 60–70% take rate.
The hosts say developing cost him almost nothing because he did it himself.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated. The hosts say Clark's developing cost was almost nothing because he did it himself, but they do not give an equipment or startup budget.

acquisition.how: The described sales method was knocking on a farmer's door and presenting a print, which depends on a human. Online ordering could be added, but the hosts do not describe it.

onboarding.how: The seller needs to identify the property, capture a suitable view, and confirm what the owner wants printed.

delivery.how: The described model requires a human to fly, develop or arrange printing, and deliver a physical print.

billing.how: A payment link or online checkout could collect one-off payments, but Clark's reported process was a direct sale.

support.how: Requests for image selection, printing, or replacement would need human handling in the described model.

uk_applicability.notes: Property owners in the UK could also buy aerial photographs. The described door-to-door selling and use of aircraft or drones would need to follow UK rules and local expectations.

risks: The historical story involves flying camera-equipped model aircraft over farms; the transcript does not describe permissions, safety procedures, or privacy considerations.
The hosts themselves note that homeowners may react badly to a drone image taken without consent.
The reported 60–70% take rate is a single second-hand anecdote and may not generalize.

ideas.name: Storm debris hauling for FEMA
ideas.one_liner: Use a truck and trailer to collect storm debris and take it to a FEMA collection station for payment.
ideas.business_model: Hypothetical per-pound payment for debris collected after a storm.
ideas.customer: FEMA or a storm cleanup program; the hosts describe residents' debris being collected through a FEMA station.
ideas.problem: Storm-damaged neighborhoods need large volumes of debris cleared.
ideas.offer: Build up the sides of a trailer, load brush and other debris densely, transport it to a weigh station, and receive payment based on weight and an estimated density factor.

pricing.model: Per-pound payment in the speaker's illustrative example.

price_points.label: Illustrative rate used in the story, not recalled as an actual rate

pricing.notes: The speaker explicitly says he does not remember the actual amount and uses $1 per pound as an example.

acquisition_channels.details: The speaker describes going into affected neighborhoods, collecting available debris, and taking it to the FEMA station. No formal contract or customer-acquisition process is described.

ideas.delivery: A person drives a truck with an open-top trailer into affected neighborhoods, loads brush and debris, takes the trailer to a weigh station, unloads it with a skid steer, and returns to collect more. The speaker says he did this as a teenager and describes the process from memory.
unit_economics_claims: The speaker's hypothetical example uses $1 per pound, 1,200 pounds before unloading, 400 pounds after unloading, and 800 pounds of debris; it then applies an estimated density percentage.
The speaker uses an illustrative $800 calculation before the density adjustment and does not give a confirmed actual payment rate.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated. The speaker says the setup involved a cheap trailer but gives no cost.

acquisition.how: The described work depended on a person finding debris in affected neighborhoods and hauling it to a collection station.

onboarding.how: The transcript does not describe formal customer onboarding; participation and payment would depend on the cleanup program's process.

delivery.how: Driving, loading, transporting, and unloading debris are physical tasks that require people and equipment.

billing.how: The speaker describes weigh-station calculations and a check, but no software-based payment process.

support.how: Disputes about weighing, density, or payment would likely need human handling; no support process is stated.

uk_applicability.notes: The example depends on a FEMA debris payment setup and disaster-response process described in the United States. A UK version would depend on different public procurement and cleanup arrangements.

risks: The speaker says the per-pound rate is only an example and does not remember the actual rate.
The story describes a person estimating trailer density; the transcript does not explain how payment calculations were audited.
Work depends on storm cleanup demand, access to a collection program, and safe loading and transport of debris.

ideas.business_model: Possible lead fees or referral fees; no model is confirmed.

ideas.problem: Roofers need to find properties that may have storm damage and potential repair work.
ideas.offer: Fly over an affected area, identify roofs that may need attention, and send leads or imagery to a roofing company. The hosts discuss having roofing contacts in place before a storm.

pricing.model: Not stated; the hosts suggest a possible referral relationship.
pricing.notes: The separate suggestion of a 30% referral fee concerns a hypothetical partner referring customers to the drone operator, not a confirmed lead-generation price.

acquisition_channels.details: Build relationships with roofing businesses before a storm so the operator can offer imagery or leads when one hits.

The hosts say roofing companies may cold-message people in an affected area. They do not say the drone operator has done this. In the UK, unsolicited messages to individuals and sole traders require care under PECR.

ideas.delivery: A drone operator captures imagery, identifies possible damage, and passes the information to a roofing company. The transcript does not explain how damage would be verified or how homeowners would consent to contact.
unit_economics_claims: The hosts suggest a possible 30% referral fee for a partner who introduces customers to the drone business; no lead-generation revenue is stated.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated; would likely use the drone equipment from the main inspection business, according to the hosts' framing.

onboarding.how: A roofing company could submit an area and lead criteria online, but the transcript does not specify a process.

delivery.how: Flying the drone and checking suspected roof damage require a person on site.

billing.how: A lead or referral fee could be tracked in software, but no agreed fee structure is described.

support.how: Software could track lead status, while disputes about damage, consent, and lead quality need human attention.

uk_applicability.notes: Storm damage and roofing demand also exist in the UK, but the transcript's practices and referral model are not validated for UK law. Outreach to individuals and sole traders must comply with UK marketing rules.

risks: The idea is speculative in the conversation and has no tested process or stated revenue.
A roof seen from the air may not have confirmed damage; passing unverified claims could harm trust.
The speakers describe cold messaging people after storms; unsolicited electronic marketing to individuals and sole traders in the UK is restricted without consent.
Flights, images, and sharing data about identifiable properties raise aviation, privacy, and consent questions.

tactics.name: Start with people already in the target industries
steps: Write down names of people you already know in real estate, construction management, roofing, insurance, property management, solar, restoration, engineering, facilities, or schools.
Ask a relevant contact for an introduction or a first job.
Prioritize a partner who can refer repeat work over a one-off customer.

tactics.name: Use outsourced drone work to practice
steps: Find companies that farm out local drone jobs.
Take operator work to build flight experience and learn the delivery process.
Use that practice before taking responsibility for a direct customer job.

tactics.name: Prepare each flight before arriving
steps: Check whether the site is in regulated airspace and request approval when needed.
Check the weather and understand the roof or site layout using Google Maps.
Arrive early and check equipment.
Capture the data, export and upload files, run the analysis, and review the final deliverable.

tactics.name: Build local search visibility
steps: Create a website with service-specific keywords and pages for named cities.
Fully complete the Google Business Profile with photos and videos.
Ask every customer for a review after a job.
Test narrower terms such as drone facade inspection against broad roof inspection terms.

tactics.name: Ask for the review while the customer is present
steps: After the job, ask whether the customer was satisfied.
If they say yes, ask them to leave a review immediately.
Politely wait while they use their phone, rather than relying on a later reminder.
When a partner referred the job, ask the partner for a review as well.

tactics.name: Test paid acquisition with a small budget
steps: Test a service and message with a limited Google or Facebook Ads budget.
Measure lead cost and close rate.
Adjust the message or target terms before increasing spend.

tactics.name: Publish repeatable drone footage
steps: Save short clips from normal jobs.
Post visually clear drone footage and before-and-after examples on social platforms and YouTube.
Reuse suitable clips on the website and local search pages.

tactics.name: Land with an inspection and expand into adjacent services
steps: Win a core inspection or documentation job with a property or construction business.
Offer social-media footage from the same visit.
Offer recurring construction-site material documentation where it fits.
Use the existing relationship to identify other adjacent needs.

tactics.name: Build storm relationships before a storm
steps: Develop relationships with roofing businesses before severe weather arrives.
When a storm affects an area, coordinate with those businesses on imagery or documentation needs.
Do not assume an aerial view proves damage; agree how leads will be verified and shared.

tactics.name: Sell a physical aerial print
steps: Capture a distinctive image of a property while doing permitted work.
Show the owner a finished print and make a clear one-off offer.
Get the owner's permission before flying over or photographing a home.

tactics.name: Load debris densely and follow the station's weighing process
steps: Use a trailer suited to the debris and build up its sides as described in the story.
Load brush densely, take the trailer to the weigh station, and follow the program's unloading and weighing process.
Confirm the actual rate and density calculation before relying on the example economics.

warnings.warning: The market size, growth, vacancy, margin, and customer-acquisition figures are claims from the hosts' research or second-hand accounts; the video does not provide source citations.

The hosts say that in some US states calling the service an inspection can trigger additional licensing requirements. Check applicable UK rules before using the term or offering regulated inspection work.

quote.speaker: Nick

warnings.warning: The transcript describes flight approvals, weather checks, insurance, and safe operation as necessary parts of delivery; skipping them could create safety and licensing problems.
Metal roofs can interfere with the drone signal, according to the hosts' account of an operator's experience.

quote.text: Metal roofs. It's just a whole different animal because you get interference with the signal.
quote.speaker: Nick

warnings.warning: The hosts describe confrontational onlookers, reporting risk, and filming from the sidewalk. Operators still need to respect privacy, permissions, and the rules that apply to each flight.

warnings.warning: The hosts say a solo operator may handle only about two roofs a day after travel, preparation, analysis, file handling, and administration.
Storm jobs can bring substantial reported revenue but may be uneven and require travel; the hosts say one operator may chase storms several hours away.

The video includes a paid TK Owners community promotion and a free newsletter and podcast promotion. These create a promotional interest even though the hosts joke about not selling a course.

warnings.warning: The hosts describe cold messaging people in storm-affected areas. In the UK, unsolicited electronic marketing to individuals and sole traders is restricted without consent.

lessons.lesson: Start with a service that solves a clear, costly problem and has repeat customers, rather than relying only on novelty.

quote.text: Technology is not changing overnight on what's required in a roof inspection. The delivery mechanism might change, but we all still need roof inspections.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: A side business can be tested alongside a job; use early jobs to gain experience before making a larger commitment.

quote.text: You don't have to quit your job and go full-time. You can start doing a couple of these a month, get the experience, and make some real money.

lessons.lesson: For an early-stage business, focus first on getting customers and delivering reliably; additional management complexity comes later.

quote.text: in the beginning, it's just can I get business and can I fulfill it?

lessons.lesson: A modest licensing and training requirement can discourage casual competitors while remaining manageable for a determined founder.

lessons.lesson: Use a core service to earn trust, then offer adjacent work that uses information or footage already collected.

lessons.lesson: Relationships with organizations that can refer recurring work may be more valuable than finding isolated one-off customers.

evidence_quality.rationale: The video is a co-host research discussion rather than an interview with a drone-inspection operator. It includes useful process detail and figures, but most operating results, market statistics, prices, margins, and ad performance are second-hand or uncited. The detailed Tom Powers example is reported by a host rather than verified in the transcript.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: The hosts promote the TK Owners paid community and their newsletter and podcast. They also joke about selling a course.
